title: The Laboratory at Spinner's End
subtitle: After Always · Chapter 37 of 40
content:
The first wall came down on a Saturday.

Not the house wall. Severus would have murdered me, survived Azkaban, and argued the conviction on grammatical grounds if I had suggested knocking through his sitting room without a structural survey.

The wall belonged to the old coal shed behind Spinner's End.

It had been leaning for years with the exhausted determination of something too stubborn to collapse while Severus was watching. We had decided the shed could become a proper laboratory annex: separate ventilation, reinforced floor, warded storage, running water, emergency exit, and enough distance from the kitchen that an exploding cauldron would not season dinner.

I had expected Severus to hire builders.

He hired builders.

Then he stood over them like an avenging gargoyle until the foreman finally put down his measuring tape and said, “Professor, either you let us do the work or you do it yourself.”

Severus considered this.

I caught his sleeve.

“We are paying them.”

“They are six millimeters off the plan.”

“They haven't built the wall yet.”

“They are contemplating it incorrectly.”

The foreman stared at me.

I stared back with the exhausted solidarity of someone who had chosen this man voluntarily.

“I'll keep him inside,” I promised.

“You will do no such thing,” Severus said.

Five minutes later he was inside.

He stood at the kitchen window with his arms crossed while masonry crashed outside.

“I dislike them.”

“They're competent.”

“A separate issue.”

I pushed a mug of coffee toward him. He had slowly, grudgingly admitted that tea was not the only civilized hot beverage in existence. He still behaved as though this concession might be used against him in court.

On the table between us lay the plans for the laboratory.

They were his plans, though my notes covered the margins. Fume hood. Isolation cupboard. Two-person ward release for the most dangerous ingredients. Accessible emergency shutoffs from either side of the room. Inventory ledger duplicated magically and on paper. No unmarked storage, no private cursed cache, no experimental substances without a second person knowing they existed.

The safeguards were not because I distrusted him.

They were because I trusted what we had learned.

Secrets had saved lives during the war.

Secrets had also nearly killed us after it.

“You moved the restricted cabinet,” he said.

“Three feet.”

“Why?”

“So if someone collapses by the main bench, the cabinet door can still open without hitting them.”

He looked at the plan.

Then at me.

Then back at the plan.

“Annoyingly sensible.”

“Put it on my gravestone.”

His face changed.

Only slightly. Anyone else might have missed it.

I did not.

“Bad joke?” I asked.

“Poorly timed.”

I reached across the table and placed my hand palm-up beside his. Not touching. Offering.

After a moment, he set his fingers into mine.

The scar at his throat was paler now, but some mornings his voice still rasped. Some evenings his left hand shook when he was tired. Healing had become less dramatic and more annoying, which Madam Pomfrey had declared an excellent sign.

I traced one knuckle with my thumb.

“I'm not planning on needing the gravestone soon.”

“You have demonstrated a troubling attraction to hazardous professionals.”

“One hazardous professional.”

“Questionable judgment remains questionable judgment even when specific.”

Outside, another section of wall crashed down.

Severus winced.

“I can hear you mentally correcting their mortar ratio.”

“It is wrong.”

“You are looking through glass from twenty feet away.”

“It is visibly wrong.”

I laughed, and his thumb rubbed once over the side of my hand.

That gesture still did things to me I refused to dignify with analysis.

On the third day, the foreman arrived with a second set of plans.

“The drainage isn't where the first drawing says,” he told us. “We opened the ground and found a pipe running straight across your proposed storage wall.”

Severus took the paper from him and inspected the measurements. “That pipe has no business being there.”

“It's been there forty years,” the foreman said. “Seems fairly committed.”

I bit my cheek. Severus could terrorize a classroom with a single raised eyebrow, but the pipe was proving immune.

He wanted to redirect it immediately. The foreman told him the neighboring kitchen shared the line; any work needed permission from the woman next door. She was home, watching the proceedings from behind her curtains.

“Did you know about the connection?” I asked Severus.

“No.” The answer sounded personally offensive to him.

We knocked on the neighbor's door together. She listened, declined the proposed afternoon shutdown, and suggested Tuesday when she would be visiting her sister.

Severus began to explain the obvious importance of his laboratory. I touched his sleeve.

“She already offered a day,” I whispered.

He stopped. Then he asked what the disruption would cost her, including the food she would need to move. He added it to the contractor's written estimate instead of assuming a neighbor should subsidize his work with inconvenience.

Inside, the kettle clicked as it cooled. I watched him stand over the revised plan, furious at a plumbing diagram and careful not to make the fury somebody else's problem.

“I understand why you never became an architect,” I said.

“An architect would have put the pipe in the correct place.”

“You're describing a miracle, not a profession.”

He snorted. Later, when the laborers arrived for the planned work, he had tea waiting for them. It was bitter enough to strip paint and served in clean cups. The foreman drank it without comment.


The laboratory took six weeks.

During that time, Severus taught his seminar, consulted twice for St. Mungo's, and revised an article on antivenom interactions so aggressively that the editor sent back a note asking whether three pages of criticism were strictly necessary.

“They asked for peer review,” he said when I pointed this out.

“They asked whether the conclusions were supported.”

“They were not.”

“You also corrected their comma placement.”

“Accuracy should not be compartmentalized.”

I kissed his cheek.

He lost his place in the manuscript.

I considered that a public service.

When the laboratory was finally finished, the builders refused to let Severus inspect it until they had packed their tools.

Cowards, but intelligent ones.

We entered together.

The room smelled of new wood, stone dust, metal, and the faint herbal bite of wards settling into place. Wide counters ran along two walls. Ingredient drawers were labeled in Severus's handwriting because he had rejected mine as “cheerful to the point of negligence.” The central island held two cauldron stations with independent heat controls. A deep sink occupied the far corner beneath a window that looked toward the narrow strip of sky above the neighboring roofs.

It was not beautiful in the conventional sense.

It was better.

It was usable.

It was safe.

It was ours without requiring either of us to disappear into the other.

Severus walked slowly through the room, touching almost nothing.

At the restricted cabinet he tested the two-person ward. His wand released one side. Mine released the other. The doors opened with a soft click.

“Functional,” he said.

“That is the most romantic thing you've ever said.”

“Your standards are catastrophic.”

“Who am I dating?”

His look should have stripped varnish.

I grinned.

On the central table sat one final object covered by a cloth.

Severus noticed immediately.

“What is that?”

“Something I had made.”

Suspicion sharpened his face. “Why?”

“Because I enjoy danger.”

I pulled away the cloth.

A brass plaque rested underneath.

Not Professor Severus Snape.

Not Headmaster.

Not Half-Blood Prince.

Not war hero, spy, traitor, Death Eater, Order member, murderer, savior, victim, bully, or any of the other names the world had used as if one noun could finish him.

It read:

SPINNER'S END POTIONS LABORATORY
S. SNAPE & ASSOCIATE
RESEARCH — ANTIDOTES — CONSULTATION

He stared at it for so long I became uncertain.

“I left myself unnamed,” I said. “On purpose. It can stay that way unless I ever want otherwise. I thought—”

“I know what you thought.”

His voice was rough.

I stopped.

He lifted the plaque with both hands.

“Associate,” he said.

“You object?”

“Profoundly.”

I blinked.

He set the plaque down.

“You are not my assistant.”

“I know.”

“Nor an adjunct to my reputation.”

“I know.”

His eyes met mine. “Partner.”

My chest tightened.

“In work?”

“In this room,” he said. Then, with the expression of a man voluntarily stepping off a cliff, “And elsewhere, should you continue to insist upon it.”

I laughed softly. “I have been fairly insistent.”

“Pathologically.”

I found a pencil and crossed out ASSOCIATE.

He watched me write PARTNER underneath.

It was crooked.

He took the pencil from me and rewrote it neatly.

“Control problem,” I said.

“Penmanship problem.”

“We can have both.”

He put the pencil down.

Then he kissed me in the middle of the empty laboratory.

There was no urgency in it. No near-death terror. No argument to propel us across a line we had been circling. Just his hand at the back of my neck, my fingers curled lightly into the front of his shirt, and the strange ordinary miracle of being able to take our time.

When we separated, I rested my forehead against his.

“Functional?” I whispered.

His eyes closed.

“Barely.”

Outside, one of the builders shouted that they had forgotten a bucket.

Severus opened his eyes with murder in them.

I laughed so hard I had to hold onto him.

He complained all the way to the door.

He did not let go of my hand.
